claim: MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells are highly invasive and aggressive in vitro and in vivo.
source: The human breast cancer cells MDA-MB-231 are highly invasive and aggressive in vitro and in vivo, and represent an ideal cellular model to study metastasis (Cailleau et al., 1974).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cailleau et al., 1974

claim: CM did not affect cell viability of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: We ascertained that CM did not affect cell viability, by verifying the incorporation of Calcein AM (viability dye), and by showing that apoptosis-triggering cytochrome c was not released by the mitochondria of CM cells, as it co-localized with COX IV (mitochondrial marker) (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by Calcein AM staining data shown in Figure 1B and cytochrome c/COX IV colocalization in Figure 1C

claim: CM-challenged MDA-MB-231 cells did not activate apoptotic effector caspases.
source: Recovered cells were viable and had not activated apoptotic effector caspases (Figure 1D), substantiating our previous result.
evidence: Supported by caspase reporter data shown in Figure 1D

claim: CM cells have a negligible proportion of cells in subG1 phase right after constriction.
source: In a complementary approach, we determined cell cycle distribution and found that CM cells have a negligible proportion of cells in subG1 (apoptotic cells) right after constriction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D)
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D

claim: CM cells have a slight arrest in G1 phase.
source: while they have a slight arrest in G1 phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), this does not affect the overall cellular proliferation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: CM does not affect overall cellular proliferation of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: while they have a slight arrest in G1 phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), this does not affect the overall cellular proliferation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1E

claim: CM cells displayed an unaltered mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: In line with this, CM cells displayed an unaltered mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP production and did not generate excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial membrane potential data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: CM cells displayed unaltered ATP production.
source: In line with this, CM cells displayed an unaltered mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP production and did not generate excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: Supported by ATP production data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: CM cells did not generate excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: In line with this, CM cells displayed an unaltered mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP production and did not generate excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: Supported by ROS measurement data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-I

claim: CM-challenged MDA-MB-231 cells survived and formed clonogenic structures in low attachment conditions more efficiently than control cells.
source: Importantly, CM-challenged MDA-MB-231 cells survived, grew, and formed clonogenic structures in low attachment conditions, as evidenced by the spheres generated, more efficiently than control cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 1F

claim: CM-challenged Hs578T breast cancer cells developed more colonies than control counterparts in low attachment conditions.
source: The effect was not restricted to MDA-MB-231 cells since CM-challenged Hs578T breast cancer cells also developed more colonies than control counterparts, indicating that CM-challenged cells had overcome anoikis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by clonogenic assay data for Hs578T cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J

claim: CM-challenged cells had overcome anoikis.
source: The effect was not restricted to MDA-MB-231 cells since CM-challenged Hs578T breast cancer cells also developed more colonies than control counterparts, indicating that CM-challenged cells had overcome anoikis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Inferred from increased colony formation in low attachment conditions shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1J

claim: CM-challenged cells show increased survival when grown in soft agar.
source: This is also the case when cells are grown in soft agar, in an anchorage-independent manner (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Breast cancer cells undergoing CM had a survival advantage when grown in low attachment conditions as assessed by real-time imaging.
source: In addition, resistance to anoikis was assessed by IncuCyte Imager-based real-time imaging, using SYTOX Green dye exclusion, and again breast cancer cells undergoing CM had a survival advantage when grown in low attachment conditions (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: Supported by IncuCyte imaging data shown in Figure 1H, I

claim: Resistance to anoikis following CM was transient.
source: MDA-MB-231 cells were challenged by CM once and anoikis resistance was quantified at 3, 5, and 7 days post-CM, revealing that resistance to anoikis was transient (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1J

claim: CM-challenged cancer cells had lower caspase-3 processing into the active p17 and p19 fragments.
source: Strikingly, CM-challenged cancer cells had lower caspase-3 processing into the active p17 and p19 fragments, whereas PARP-1 cleavage followed the same pattern (Figure 1K, L).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1K, L

claim: PARP-1 cleavage was reduced in CM-challenged cancer cells.
source: Strikingly, CM-challenged cancer cells had lower caspase-3 processing into the active p17 and p19 fragments, whereas PARP-1 cleavage followed the same pattern (Figure 1K, L).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1K, L

claim: Lower effector caspase activation in CM cells was confirmed using a fluorometric caspase-3/7 assay.
source: Lower effector caspase activation was also confirmed using a fluorometric caspase-3/7 assay, demonstrating that inhibition was particularly important for cells grown in ultra-low attachment and soft agar conditions (further designated as anoikis-favouring conditions) (Figure 1M).
evidence: Supported by fluorometric caspase assay data shown in Figure 1M

claim: Caspase inhibition was particularly important for CM cells grown in anoikis-favouring conditions.
source: Lower effector caspase activation was also confirmed using a fluorometric caspase-3/7 assay, demonstrating that inhibition was particularly important for cells grown in ultra-low attachment and soft agar conditions (further designated as anoikis-favouring conditions) (Figure 1M).
evidence: Supported by fluorometric caspase assay data shown in Figure 1M

claim: Compression did not affect resistance to anoikis in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Resistance to anoikis, as assessed by growing these cells in anoikis-favouring conditions, was not modified under compression (Figure 1N, O), suggesting that acquisition of resistance to anoikis may be specific to CM.
evidence: Supported by compression experiment data shown in Figure 1N, O

claim: Acquisition of resistance to anoikis may be specific to CM.
source: Resistance to anoikis, as assessed by growing these cells in anoikis-favouring conditions, was not modified under compression (Figure 1N, O), suggesting that acquisition of resistance to anoikis may be specific to CM.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of CM and compression effects on anoikis resistance shown in Figure 1N, O

claim: Cancer cell migration through 8 µm in diameter microporous transwells did not confer cancer cells with resistance to anoikis.
source: In addition, cancer cell migration through 8 µm in diameter microporous transwells, which does not impose cellular constriction, did not confer cancer cells with resistance to anoikis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M, N) and had no impact on caspase activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: Supported by 8 µm transwell experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1M, N

claim: Migration through 8 µm transwells had no impact on caspase activation.
source: In addition, cancer cell migration through 8 µm in diameter microporous transwells, which does not impose cellular constriction, did not confer cancer cells with resistance to anoikis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M, N) and had no impact on caspase activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: Supported by caspase activation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1O

claim: The expression of BCL-xL, BCL2, and MCL1 was unchanged in CM cells.
source: Of note, the expression of several anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL-xL, BCL2, and MCL1 was unchanged in CM cells, suggesting another resistance mechanism to anoikis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1P

claim: CM-driven resistance to anoikis suggests a mechanism other than upregulation of BCL-xL, BCL2, and MCL1.
source: Of note, the expression of several anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL-xL, BCL2, and MCL1 was unchanged in CM cells, suggesting another resistance mechanism to anoikis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: Inferred from unchanged expression of BCL-xL, BCL2, and MCL1 shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1P

claim: IAPs such as cIAP1, cIAP2, and XIAP promote resistance to anoikis in several cancers through caspase inhibition.
source: Previous studies reported that IAPs such as cIAP1, cIAP2, and XIAP promote resistance to anoikis in several cancers, through caspase inhibition (Toruner et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2006; Berezovskaya et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Toruner et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2006; Berezovskaya et al., 2005

claim: CM MDA-MB-231 cells grown in anoikis-favouring conditions showed an upregulation of cIAP1, cIAP2, and XIAP.
source: This was tested by immunoblotting for cIAP1, cIAP2, and XIAP protein expression in CM MDA-MB-231 cells grown in anoikis-favouring conditions, which revealed an upregulation of all three IAPs (Figure 2A, left panel for densitometry analysis).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: MDA-MB-231 cells subjected to compression had unaltered levels of IAPs.
source: Conversely, MDA-MB-231 cells subjected to compression or migration through 8 µm in diameter microporous transwells had unaltered levels of IAPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: MDA-MB-231 cells subjected to migration through 8 µm in diameter microporous transwells had unaltered levels of IAPs.
source: Conversely, MDA-MB-231 cells subjected to compression or migration through 8 µm in diameter microporous transwells had unaltered levels of IAPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Enforced expression of cIAP1 significantly enhanced resistance to anoikis in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Enforced expression of cIAP1 and XIAP significantly enhanced resistance to anoikis in cells grown under anoikis-favouring conditions, while cIAP2 overexpression was dispensable (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by overexpression experiment data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Enforced expression of XIAP significantly enhanced resistance to anoikis in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Enforced expression of cIAP1 and XIAP significantly enhanced resistance to anoikis in cells grown under anoikis-favouring conditions, while cIAP2 overexpression was dispensable (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by overexpression experiment data shown in Figure 2E

claim: cIAP2 overexpression was dispensable for resistance to anoikis in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Enforced expression of cIAP1 and XIAP significantly enhanced resistance to anoikis in cells grown under anoikis-favouring conditions, while cIAP2 overexpression was dispensable (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by overexpression experiment data shown in Figure 2D

claim: IAP-depleted MDA-MB-231 cells lost their survival advantage following CM and growth in anoikis-favouring conditions.
source: Following CM and growth in anoikis-favouring conditions, control cells (EV) displayed the expected resistance to anoikis, whereas IAP-depleted cells lost their survival advantage (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by CRISPR knockout experiment data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: BV6 SMAC mimetic successfully depleted both cIAP1 and XIAP.
source: In addition, the use of a SMAC mimetic, one of several developed to specifically induce IAP degradation, namely BV6, successfully depleted both cIAP1 and XIAP (Figure 2H; Varfolomeev et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2H and citation to Varfolomeev et al., 2007

claim: BV6 SMAC mimetic abrogated the resistance to anoikis observed in CM-challenged breast cancer cells.
source: Interestingly, it also abrogated the resistance to anoikis observed in CM-challenged breast cancer cells (Figure 2I, J).
evidence: Supported by BV6 treatment experiment data shown in Figure 2I, J

claim: IAPs mRNA expression was not increased in CM cells compared to control cells.
source: We initially performed qRT-PCR analysis to assess IAPs mRNA expression in CM cells and uncovered that their transcript expression was not increased compared to control cells, with a significant inhibition observed for cIAP2 and XIAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: cIAP2 and XIAP mRNA expression was significantly inhibited in CM cells.
source: We initially performed qRT-PCR analysis to assess IAPs mRNA expression in CM cells and uncovered that their transcript expression was not increased compared to control cells, with a significant inhibition observed for cIAP2 and XIAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Constricted cells displayed an accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins.
source: Constricted cells displayed an accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, indicating a possible bottleneck for protein degradation in CM-stressed cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by K48-ubiquitin Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: XIAP protein showed a slower decrease in CM cells compared to control cells in cycloheximide chase assay.
source: When focusing on XIAP, which was the most differentially expressed IAP in CM-challenged cells, we observed a slower decrease in XIAP protein in CM cells compared to control cells, suggesting a lower proteasomal degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: XIAP may be more stable in CM cells.
source: XIAP may thus be more stable in CM cells, which might explain its higher expression following CM.
evidence: Inferred from cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: CM increases p65 nuclear translocation in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: To test whether CM activates NF-κB, we first assessed p65 translocation from the cytoplasm to the nucleus upon CM, and showed an increase in cells displaying nuclear p65 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: CM increases NF-κB transcriptional activity.
source: Using two luciferase-based NF-κB reporter constructs, CM was also found to increase NF-κB transcriptional activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I

claim: Blocking the NF-κB pathway in CM cells did not prevent their resistance to anoikis.
source: However, in these settings, blocking the NF-κB pathway in CM cells did not prevent their resistance to anoikis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K,L ).
evidence: Supported by IκBSR expression experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K, L

claim: TNFα treatment can upregulate cIAP2 but had no effect on cIAP1 and XIAP.
source: In addition, the artificial activation of NF-κB pathway using TNFα treatment, can upregulate cIAP2 as previously described, yet it had no effect on both cIAP1 and XIAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1M, N; Diessenbacher et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by TNFα treatment experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1M, N and citation to Diessenbacher et al., 2008

claim: CM-driven mechanical stress is characterized by NF-κB activation, which is not involved in the survival advantage observed in CM-challenged cancer cells.
source: These data suggest that CM-driven mechanical stress is characterized by NF-κB activation, which is not involved in the survival advantage observed in CM-challenged cancer cells.
evidence: Inferred from IκBSR blocking experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K, L

claim: IAPs high expressing cells (EV cells) showed the same CM capacity as IAPs KO cells.
source: As shown in Figure 2L, the score was similar to the initial 50:50 ratio, with IAPs high expressing cells (the EV cells) showing the same CM capacity as IAPs KO cells.
evidence: Supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 2L

claim: CM does not select for cells having a different expression of IAPs.
source: These results imply that CM is not selecting for cells having a different expression of IAPs or displaying resistance to anoikis.
evidence: Inferred from competition assay data shown in Figure 2L, N

claim: CM does not select for cells displaying resistance to anoikis.
source: These results imply that CM is not selecting for cells having a different expression of IAPs or displaying resistance to anoikis.
evidence: Inferred from competition assay data shown in Figure 2N

claim: Resistance to anoikis driven by CM mechanical stress relies on the pro-survival function of IAPs, regulated at the post-transcriptional level following mechanical stress.
source: To conclude, resistance to anoikis driven by CM mechanical stress relies on the pro-survival function of IAPs, regulated at the post-transcriptional level following mechanical stress.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing IAP upregulation at protein but not mRNA level, and functional rescue experiments

claim: CM cells displayed an almost global inhibition of transcription.
source: Remarkably, CM cells displayed an almost global inhibition of transcription, making their transcriptional profile distinct from control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: CM cells had a lower histone H3 acetylation.
source: Consistently with their overall transcriptional inhibition, CM cells had a lower histone H3 acetylation and a reduction in heterochromatin (lower H3K9 me3), which may indicate a decrease in nuclear stiffness, which is needed when cells navigate through narrow spaces (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: CM cells had a reduction in heterochromatin (lower H3K9 me3).
source: Consistently with their overall transcriptional inhibition, CM cells had a lower histone H3 acetylation and a reduction in heterochromatin (lower H3K9 me3), which may indicate a decrease in nuclear stiffness, which is needed when cells navigate through narrow spaces (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Reduced H3K9 me3 in CM cells may indicate a decrease in nuclear stiffness.
source: Consistently with their overall transcriptional inhibition, CM cells had a lower histone H3 acetylation and a reduction in heterochromatin (lower H3K9 me3), which may indicate a decrease in nuclear stiffness, which is needed when cells navigate through narrow spaces (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Speculated based on histone modification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and established knowledge about chromatin and nuclear stiffness

claim: Several pathways associated with cellular motility such as 'Extracellular matrix organization', 'Cell-matrix adhesion', or 'Cell adhesion' were significantly overrepresented in CM cells.
source: When querying the Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Processes using both Enrichr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and g:Profiler (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), several pathways associated with cellular motility such as 'Extracellular matrix organization', 'Cell-matrix adhesion', or 'Cell adhesion' were significantly overrepresented in CM cells (Chen et al., 2013; Raudvere et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E and citations to Chen et al., 2013; Raudvere et al., 2019

claim: Cancer cells subjected to CM had an increased number of stress fibres.
source: This revealed an increased number of stress fibres following CM, in addition to more abundant filopodia (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by F-actin staining data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Cancer cells subjected to CM had more abundant filopodia.
source: This revealed an increased number of stress fibres following CM, in addition to more abundant filopodia (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by F-actin staining data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Cancer cells subjected to CM had a higher variation in cell area over time.
source: By using Nanolive imager-based cellular tomography, we uncovered that cancer cells subjected to CM had a higher variation in cell area over time (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by Nanolive imaging data shown in Figure 3B

claim: CM-challenged cancer cells displayed a significantly higher velocity than control cells.
source: CM-challenged cancer cells displayed a significantly higher velocity and travelled further than control cells (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by single-cell migration tracking data shown in Figure 3C-E

claim: CM-challenged cancer cells travelled further than control cells.
source: CM-challenged cancer cells displayed a significantly higher velocity and travelled further than control cells (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by single-cell migration tracking data shown in Figure 3C-E

claim: The increased single-cell migration observed in CM cells was not correlated with the number of focal adhesions.
source: The increased single-cell migration observed was not correlated with the number of focal adhesions.
evidence: Inferred from focal adhesion quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: Breast cancer cells subjected to a single round of CM did not outperform control cells in collective cell migration and invasion.
source: In contrast to single-cell migration, breast cancer cells subjected to a single round of CM did not outperform control cells when assessed by collective cell migration and invasion (Figure 3F–K).
evidence: Supported by wound healing and invasion assay data shown in Figure 3F-K

claim: MDA-MB-231 cells subjected to three consecutive CM passages had a significant gain in chemotaxis and collective cell migration.
source: As cells encounter several mechanical challenges during metastasis, we then imposed three consecutive CM passages on MDA-MB-231 cells, and found that challenged cells had a significant gain in chemotaxis and collective cell migration (Figure 3L–N, experimental setup in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by serial CM experiment data shown in Figure 3L-N

claim: MDA-MB-231 cells with higher levels of lamin A have a lower capacity to perform CM.
source: Confirming previous studies, we also found that MDA-MB-231 cells with higher levels of lamin A have a lower capacity to perform CM, most probably due to increased nuclear stiffness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by lamin A overexpression competition assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J and citations to previous studies

claim: The expression of lamin A/C in cancer cells right after CM was similar to that found in control cells.
source: Yet, when the expression of lamin A/C was tested in cancer cells right after CM, it was similar to that found in control cells, implying once more that CM does not select for cells with certain characteristics, such as lower expression of lamins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K

claim: CM does not select for cells with lower expression of lamins.
source: Yet, when the expression of lamin A/C was tested in cancer cells right after CM, it was similar to that found in control cells, implying once more that CM does not select for cells with certain characteristics, such as lower expression of lamins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Inferred from lamin A/C expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K

claim: Breast cancer cells were partially protected from NK-mediated cytotoxicity following CM.
source: Interestingly, breast cancer cells were partially protected from the NK-mediated cytotoxicity following CM (Figure 3O, CFSElow population represents apoptotic cells), consistent with lower levels of toxic granzyme B incorporation (Figure 3P).
evidence: Supported by NK cell co-culture experiment data shown in Figure 3O, P

claim: CM cells showed lower levels of toxic granzyme B incorporation.
source: Interestingly, breast cancer cells were partially protected from the NK-mediated cytotoxicity following CM (Figure 3O, CFSElow population represents apoptotic cells), consistent with lower levels of toxic granzyme B incorporation (Figure 3P).
evidence: Supported by granzyme B incorporation data shown in Figure 3P

claim: A single event of CM has a profound effect on single-cell migration.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that a single event of CM has a profound effect on single-cell migration, while several rounds of CM enhance cancer cell chemotaxis and collective migration.
evidence: Inferred from single-cell migration data shown in Figure 3C-E

claim: Several rounds of CM enhance cancer cell chemotaxis and collective migration.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that a single event of CM has a profound effect on single-cell migration, while several rounds of CM enhance cancer cell chemotaxis and collective migration.
evidence: Inferred from serial CM data shown in Figure 3L-N

claim: CM contributes to evasion from NK-mediated immune surveillance.
source: In addition, CM contributes to evasion from NK-mediated immune surveillance.
evidence: Inferred from NK cell co-culture data shown in Figure 3O, P

claim: Metastasis incidence was significantly higher for CM cells 6 weeks post-engraftment.
source: We observed that metastasis incidence was significantly higher for CM cells 6 weeks post-engraftment (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by in vivo metastasis incidence data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The volume of healthy lung tissue in mice engrafted with CM breast cancer cells was considerably smaller than control counterparts.
source: Moreover, the volume of healthy lung tissue in mice engrafted with CM breast cancer cells was considerably smaller than control counterparts, indicating their increased aggressiveness (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: Supported by microCT imaging data shown in Figure 4B, C

claim: Breast cancer cells experiencing three consecutive rounds of CM showed increased aggressiveness in vivo.
source: Of note, this was also the case for breast cancer cells experiencing three consecutive rounds of CM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: The increased aggressiveness of constricted cells was quantified by measuring the area of metastatic lesions following H&E staining.
source: In addition, the increased aggressiveness of constricted cells was also quantified by measuring the area of metastatic lesions following H&E staining (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 4D, E

claim: A single event of CM was sufficient to enhance lung metastatic colonization in mice.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that a single event of CM was sufficient to enhance lung metastatic colonization in mice.
evidence: Inferred from in vivo metastasis data shown in Figure 4A-E

claim: CM is characterized by resistance to anoikis, increased single-cell motility, NF-κB activation and escape from immune surveillance.
source: Hence, we show here that CM is characterized by resistance to anoikis, increased single-cell motility, NF-κB activation and escape from immune surveillance.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript

claim: The resistance to anoikis following CM relies on pro-survival IAPs, regulated at the post-transcriptional level following mechanical stress.
source: Although independent of NF-κB activation, the resistance to anoikis relies on pro-survival IAPs, regulated at the post-transcriptional level following mechanical stress.
evidence: Inferred from IAP expression and functional studies shown in Figure 2

claim: CM promotes cancer metastasis through resistance to anoikis and increased invasiveness.
source: Confined migration promotes cancer metastasis through resistance to anoikis and increased invasiveness
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The majority of cancer-related deaths arise following metastasis.
source: The majority of cancer-related deaths arise following metastasis (Dillekås et al., 2019; Chaffer and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dillekås et al., 2019; Chaffer and Weinberg, 2011

claim: No efficient therapeutic strategies currently prevent metastasis formation.
source: Though the mechanisms driving cancer cell migration and invasion are well documented, with a clear understanding of epithelial–mesenchymal transition and the metastatic niche, no efficient therapeutic strategies currently prevent metastasis formation (Lambert et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lambert et al., 2017

claim: Metastasis is largely incurable.
source: Metastasis is thus largely incurable, yet this lengthy process can take years and the therapeutic window is therefore large enough to envisage its targeting (Mehlen and Puisieux, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mehlen and Puisieux, 2006 and established clinical knowledge

claim: Compressive forces on cancer cells can reach up to 10kPa in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
source: During early tumour development, excessive cell proliferation, massive extracellular matrix deposition, or cancer-associated fibroblasts exert compressive forces on cancer cells that can reach up to 10kPa in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (Nia et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nia et al., 2016

claim: CM can break the nuclear envelope and trigger DNA damage and mutagenesis if the breaks are not efficiently repaired.
source: These events, known as confined migration (CM), have dramatic consequences on cancer cells and might even break the nuclear envelope and trigger DNA damage and mutagenesis if the breaks are not efficiently repaired (Raab et al., 2016; Denais et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Raab et al., 2016; Denais et al., 2016

claim: Repeated nuclear deformations and loss of nuclear envelope integrity can activate an invasive programme.
source: More precisely, repeated nuclear deformations and loss of nuclear envelope integrity can activate an invasive programme, and engage the pro-oncogenic Ras/MAPK signalling pathway (Nader et al., 2021; Rudzka et al., 2021; Rudzka et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nader et al., 2021; Rudzka et al., 2021; Rudzka et al., 2019

claim: Most CTCs are eliminated by apoptosis in a process called anoikis.
source: Moreover, most CTCs are eliminated by apoptosis in a process called anoikis, occurring when cells detach from the extracellular matrix (Shen and Kang, 2020; Paoli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen and Kang, 2020; Paoli et al., 2013

claim: Anoikis has evolved as an efficient physiological barrier for preventing the formation of metastatic colonies by CTCs reaching target organs.
source: By rapidly engaging either the death receptors or the mitochondrial pathway of apoptosis, anoikis has evolved as an efficient physiological barrier for preventing the formation of metastatic colonies by CTCs reaching target organs (Shen and Kang, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shen and Kang, 2020

claim: Cancer cells developed strategies to evade anoikis such as overly activated Ras/ERK and PI3K/Akt pathways, engaging the tyrosine kinase receptor TrkB, inactivation of E-cadherin and p53 or enhanced autophagy.
source: Nonetheless, cancer cells developed strategies to evade anoikis such as overly activated Ras/ERK and PI3K/Akt pathways, engaging the tyrosine kinase receptor TrkB, inactivation of E-cadherin and p53 or enhanced autophagy (de Sousa Mesquita et al., 2017; Douma et al., 2004; Derksen et al., 2006; Fung et al., 2008; Chavez-Dominguez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Sousa Mesquita et al., 2017; Douma et al., 2004; Derksen et al., 2006; Fung et al., 2008; Chavez-Dominguez et al., 2020

claim: This is the first study showing that mechanical stress increases IAPs expression.
source: Interestingly, these proteins were described to promote resistance to anoikis in several cancers. Nevertheless this is the first study showing that mechanical stress increases IAPs expression, especially cIAP1 and XIAP, likely by modifying their protein turnover (Toruner et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2006; Berezovskaya et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a claim of novelty made by the authors based on their findings and comparison to existing literature

claim: Several SMAC mimetics such as birinapant and LCL161 are in phase two clinical trials for ovarian cancer and myeloma.
source: Currently, several SMAC mimetics such as birinapant and LCL161 are in phase two clinical trials for ovarian cancer and myeloma (source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/).
evidence: Supported by reference to clinicaltrials.gov database

claim: Resistance to anoikis could be promoted by shear stress.
source: Although it has been reported that resistance to anoikis could be promoted by shear stress, we report here for the first time that CM, a mechanical stress in the metastatic cascade happening before the fluid shear stress, can also induce resistance to anoikis in breast cancer cells (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2019
